finding: The traversal cases in C16 never reach the server as written. `fetch()` runs the URL through the WHATWG URL parser, which resolves `..` and `%2e%2e` dot-segments before sending. `/app.css/../server.js` goes out as `/server.js`, `/../src/server.js` as `/src/server.js`, and `/%2e%2e/server.js` as `/server.js`. The test therefore only shows that unrelated paths return 404. It would still pass if the static handler did path joining and was open to traversal. Only `/app.js%00.txt`, `/APP.JS` and `/client/app.js` test a real negative.
evidence: `const negativePaths = [ "/app.css/../server.js", "/%2e%2e/server.js", "/../src/server.js", "/client/app.js", "/app.js%00.txt", "/APP.JS", ]; ... const res = await fetch(\`${base}${p}\`);` (traversal strings are sent through `fetch`, not a raw `http.request`/`net` socket)

finding: The "protective" deny rules are prefix patterns on specific git/file commands, and Bash is otherwise unrestricted. A role with Bash (qa-evidence, security-privacy, backend-architect, sre and others) can still change or exfiltrate. Examples are `sed -i`, `tee`, `cat > file`, `python -c`, `node -e`, `git -C . commit`, `git -c ... push`, `git stash`, `git rebase`, `git merge`, `git tag`, `git branch -D` and `scp`. It can also read denied files, for example `cat .env` or `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa`. `Read(...)` deny rules do not cover Bash. The `git push` and `git commit` denies are weakened further by variants such as `git -C <dir> push`. The deny list gives a false sense that human-approval-gated actions (send, destructive shared-state, deploy) are blocked.
evidence: evidence: `"Bash(git push:*)", "Bash(git commit:*)", "Bash(git add:*)", ... "Bash(rm:*)", "Bash(mv:*)", "Bash(cp:*)", "Bash(curl:*)", "Bash(wget:*)"`, with no `ask` list, no `sandbox` setting and no `Bash` default restriction. The secret-read rules at lines 19-53 are all `Read(...)` only.
